title: FindRoot::jsing — symmetric seeds kill the Jacobian
body: A singular Jacobian in FindRoot almost always means degenerate/symmetric starting points (equal, opposite-pair, or zero seeds make rows dependent). Break the symmetry: give each variable a DIFFERENT, slightly irrational seed (0.37, -0.61, 1.13…), add small random perturbations, and for known-symmetric root pairs solve for the asymmetric combination (sum/difference) instead.

title: 1/0 and 0*ComplexInfinity in rational equations — clear denominators first
body: Bethe-type/rational equations blow up (Power::infy, Infinity::indet) when the solver steps onto a pole (e.g. u_i == u_j in a denominator). Multiply the equations through by their denominators BEFORE solving: polys = Numerator[Together[lhs - rhs]]; then FindRoot/NSolve the polynomial system. Also never evaluate the raw equations at coinciding roots.

title: Thread::tdlen — unequal lengths; check counts before elementwise ops
body: Thread/listable ops need equal-length lists. Check Length[a] == Length[b] BEFORE subtracting/comparing spectra — a mismatch usually means you MISSED states (or double-counted), which is a physics finding, not a formatting problem. Sort both sides and compare Tally counts first.
example: If[Length[eB] == Length[eD], Max[Abs[Sort[eB] - Sort[eD]]], {"count mismatch", Length[eB], Length[eD]}]

title: FindRoot::nveq — one seed per variable, equations as an explicit list
body: FindRoot needs the equation COUNT to match the variable count, with explicit seeds per variable. If your equations come from a function returning a vector, evaluate them into an explicit list first (Thread[f[u1,u2] == 0] // Evaluate) — a held function of the wrong arity looks like 1 equation in N variables.

title: NSolve/Solve 'not a valid variable' — the symbol already has a value
body: `0.114 is not a valid variable` means a symbol you are solving for was ASSIGNED earlier in the session. Never assign to symbols you later solve for; if it happened, Clear[u1, u2] right before the solve, or solve in fresh symbols (v1, v2) and substitute after.

title: ReplaceAll::reps — inspect solver output shape before substituting
body: Solver output is a LIST OF RULE-LISTS: vals = vars /. sols[[1]]. If you see `{False, False} is neither a list of replacements`, you substituted into booleans (you applied /. to equations, or the solve returned {} / a ConditionalExpression). Check Head and Length of the result first; {} means the solver FAILED — change method, don't substitute.
example: sols = NSolve[eqs, vars]; If[sols =!= {}, vars /. First[sols], "no solutions"]

title: Abs takes ONE argument
body: Abs[a, b] is an arity error. For tolerance tests write Abs[a - b] < 10^-8, or Chop[a - b, 10^-8] == 0 for structured values. The same applies to Norm for vectors: Norm[a - b] < tol.

title: Complex numbers have no <, and Sort on them is structural
body: Less::nord / wrong orderings: complex values cannot be compared with < and default Sort orders them structurally. Sort with an explicit numeric key: SortBy[list, {Re[#], Im[#]} &] (or N[...] first). Compare complex spectra only after such sorting on BOTH sides.

title: General::stop is not the error — scroll to the FIRST message
body: `Further output ... will be suppressed` only says an earlier message repeated 3+. The actionable error is the FIRST distinct message in the output — fix that one; the rest usually vanish with it.

title: Recorded symbols are immutable — build FORWARD, never redefine
body: The harness rejects probes that redefine a symbol an earlier recorded step already defines. Use the existing symbol BY NAME and derive new quantities into NEW symbols. If a recorded step is genuinely wrong, `invalidate` it first — silent redefinition breaks the fresh-kernel replay.

title: Near-duplicate probe rejected — change the APPROACH, not a constant
body: A probe ≥90% similar to a recent one is rejected to stop thrash. Use `amend_probe` to fix the previous probe in place. If the same approach failed twice, the third similar attempt will too: switch method (different parametrization, higher WorkingPrecision, polynomial form, smaller subproblem) instead of nudging numbers.

title: Dot::dotsh — check Dimensions on both operands
body: Dot needs compatible tensor shapes: check Dimensions[a] and Dimensions[b] before a.b. Common causes: a list-of-eigenvectors is ROWS (use v.m or m.Transpose[v] accordingly); elementwise product wants * not . ; a flattened vector where a matrix is expected.

title: Guard list ops against {} — empty solver output upstream
body: Take/First/Part on {} (Take::take, First::first) usually means an upstream solve/select returned NOTHING. Test Length[...] > 0 before extracting, and treat 'empty' as a finding: the method failed and needs changing — don't paper over it with defaults.
example: If[sols === {}, "solver returned nothing — change method", First[sols]]

title: Return[] escapes nested inline Modules — use Catch/Throw
body: Return[expr] inside an inline Module/Block propagates OUT through enclosing Modules; statements after it silently never run. For early exit use Catch[Module[..., If[bad, Throw[val]]; ...]] — Throw stops exactly at its Catch.

title: Module[{u}, …] shadows the global u your stored expressions reference
body: Module renames its locals — a stored polynomial in global `u` will NOT match a Module-local `u` (replacements silently do nothing). To temporarily clear a global's value while keeping symbol identity, use Block[{u}, ...]; or use distinct local names.

title: One Out[] per probe — end intermediate lines with ;
body: A cell with several unterminated statements prints several Out[] lines, but only the LAST expression is the cell's verifiable value. Terminate intermediate lines with `;` and make the headline result the final expression — or better, return one Association bundling the related values.

title: Near-singular numerics: raise WorkingPrecision WITH high-precision inputs
body: Machine precision fails near singular/stiff configurations. Use FindRoot/NSolve[..., WorkingPrecision -> 30] — but the inputs must ALSO be exact or high-precision (SetPrecision[x, 30] or rationals); one machine-precision constant poisons the whole computation back to MachinePrecision.

title: Probe near the 60s timeout — split it, and avoid Simplify on large expressions
body: Long-running probes should be decomposed: compute and store intermediates in separate probes (symbols persist in the kernel). Simplify/FullSimplify on large expressions is the usual sink — prefer Expand/Together/Factor, numeric checks via N, and Chop; simplify only the final small result.

title: = assigns, == is (possibly unevaluated) equality, === is definite
body: `=` ASSIGNS (a common accidental overwrite of a solver variable). `==` stays unevaluated for symbolic operands — as a check it may return neither True nor False; use === for structural identity or Simplify[lhs == rhs] / Abs[lhs - rhs] < tol for mathematical equality of expressions.
example: Simplify[expr1 - expr2] === 0   (* not expr1 == expr2 as a truth test *)

title: Eigenvalues: N[] the matrix, not the result — exact eigenvalues explode
body: Eigenvalues of an exact symbolic/rational matrix beyond ~10×10 produces giant Root[] expressions (slow, unusable). Diagonalise numerically: Eigenvalues[N[H]] (or N[H, 30] for precision), and only keep exact eigenvalues for small matrices where you need closed forms. Round/Chop for tallying degeneracies.

title: Verify conventions on a minimal known case BEFORE scaling up
body: Before building the full-size object (Hamiltonian, operator, generating function), verify your normalization/sign/shift conventions on a case with a KNOWN closed-form answer: the smallest size, a single excitation, or a textbook limit (e.g. a one-particle dispersion, a 2x2 matrix, n=1 term of a series). A wrong convention detected at full scale invalidates every downstream step and typically costs the whole backtrack budget; the minimal check costs one probe. Record the convention as a note_fact so later steps and the crosscheck use the same one.
example: H per bond (S.S - 1/4) vs S.S differ by a constant shift L/4: check the 1-magnon energy against E(k) = cos k - 1 before diagonalising the full sector.

title: Periodic wrap bond (L,1): embed via single-site operator PRODUCTS
body: For a periodic chain, never build the wrap term (L,1) by reordering KroneckerProduct factors or hand-permuting bit orders — both are the classic source of a non-translation-invariant spectrum. Express the two-site operator as a sum of PRODUCTS of single-site embeddings: h_{ij} = Sum_ab c_ab op[Ea,i].op[Eb,j] with op[m,i] = KroneckerProduct @@ ReplacePart[ConstantArray[id,L], i->m]. This works for ANY pair (i,j) including the wrap, with no special casing. Sanity check immediately: the one-particle spectrum must be symmetric under k -> -k, and the vacuum/known-limit energy must come out exactly.

title: Sort on symbolic expressions is STRUCTURAL — use SortBy[list, N]
body: Sort[] and Min/Max ordering on exact symbolic values (2(1-Sqrt[3]/2) vs 2, radicals, Root objects) compares expression STRUCTURE, not numeric value — the result silently comes out in the wrong order and downstream selections (lowest state, extremal root) pick the wrong element. Order numerically: SortBy[list, N], MinimalBy[list, N], or Sort[N[list]] when exactness of the sort keys does not matter. Same trap in Select with < or > on symbolic entries.
example: SortBy[{2 (1 - Sqrt[3]/2), 2}, N]  (* correct numeric order; plain Sort gets it wrong *)

title: ReplacePart multi-position needs {{p1},{p2}} — {p1,p2}->v is ONE nested position
body: ReplacePart[list, {1,2,3} -> v] does NOT replace elements 1,2,3 — it addresses the single NESTED position [[1,2,3]] and, when that position does not exist, silently returns the list UNCHANGED (no message). The silent no-op then propagates (e.g. every basis state stays the vacuum). For multiple positions write ReplacePart[list, {{1},{2},{3}} -> v], or avoid ReplacePart: Module[{l = list}, l[[{1,2,3}]] = v; l].

title: list[[0]] returns the HEAD (List), not an element
body: Part index 0 is the expression HEAD: list[[0]] silently returns List (or the function head) instead of erroring, so 0-based enumeration bugs corrupt sums with a literal List symbol appearing in results. WL is 1-based; when enumerating modes n=0..L-1 stored in a list, index with [[n+1]] and assert the offset once in a comment.
example: eps[[n + 1]] (* mode n, 0-based physics label, 1-based WL storage *)

title: Slot (#, #name) only works inside Function/& — elsewhere it is Protected
body: Slot syntax (#, #2, #key) is ONLY meaningful inside a Function (ending in &). Used inside Table/Do/Module bodies without &, it stays the raw Slot object and assignments to it throw 'Tag Slot is Protected' (Table::write). Use the iterator variable or a named function argument instead; for Association field access outside a Function, write assoc['key'], not #key.

title: Underscore in a name makes a PATTERN — lam_i is lam blank i, not a variable
body: WL identifiers cannot contain underscores: lam_i parses as the pattern lam_i (lam : Blank[i]), silently matching instead of storing. Same family: x[Range[6]] applies x to the whole list (one call), not elementwise — use Map or x /@ Range[6]; and iterator names reused in nested Do/Table shadow each other. Name variables camelCase (lamI), and if an expression unexpectedly contains Blank[] or Pattern[], an underscore slipped into a name.
example: lamI = {3, 2, 1}   (* lam_i would be a pattern, not an assignment *)

title: FiniteGroupData needs {"SymmetricGroup", n} — not {"Symmetric", n}
body: FiniteGroupData::notent means the ENTITY NAME is wrong, not that the data is missing. Group entities are spelled in full: {"SymmetricGroup", n}, {"AlternatingGroup", n}, {"DihedralGroup", n}, {"CyclicGroup", n}. FiniteGroupData[{"SymmetricGroup", n}, "CharacterTable"] DOES work (checked to n=10). Align its columns with FiniteGroupData[..., "ConjugacyClassNames"] (cycle-type partitions); "ConjugacyClasses" returns element indices, not cycle types. Never load Combinatorica for this — its CharacterTable clashes with modern Graph symbols.

title: Sort::normal — you passed an Association/SparseArray where a List was expected
body: Sort::normal ("Nonatomic expression expected") means the argument is an Association, SparseArray, or other non-List head. Convert explicitly first: Values[assoc] or Normal[assoc] for Associations, Normal[sa] for SparseArray. The same family of errors (First::nofirst, Part::partw, Take::take) usually means the object is EMPTY or not the shape you assumed — check Head[expr] and Length[expr] before indexing.

title: Max::meprec / $MaxExtraPrecision — stop comparing unevaluated symbolic reals
body: Max::meprec means WL is trying to decide an inequality between symbolic exact expressions and ran out of extra precision. Raising $MaxExtraPrecision only delays it. The fix is to numericise BEFORE ordering or comparing: N[expr, 30], SortBy[list, N], or Chop[N[…]] for near-zero tests. If the comparison must stay exact, use FullSimplify on the DIFFERENCE and test against 0 rather than comparing the two sides directly.
example: SortBy[vals, N]   (* or N[vals, 30] before Max/Min/Sort *)

title: SparseArray rules need {i, j} -> v positions, not nested rules
body: SparseArray::posd ("left-hand side of (1 -> 1) -> 1 is not a valid position") means a rule was built with the wrong shape — usually Thread or Map produced (i -> j) -> v instead of {i, j} -> v. Build positions as LISTS: SparseArray[{{i, j} -> v, …}, {n, n}]. For a single index use {i} -> v. Check one element of your rule list before passing the whole thing.
